2026 · Research Note 10

Can machine-learning potentials make atomistic electrochemical-interface simulations large enough to become more useful?

MACE interatomic potentials trained through active learning reproduce DFT-level behavior across 21 charged metal–electrolyte systems.

In brief

QuestionCan machine-learning potentials make atomistic electrochemical-interface simulations large enough to become more useful?
ResultThe MLIP committee models aqueous NaCl at Au, Cu, and Rh(111) interfaces over a range of surface charge densities with DFT-level accuracy.
Why it mattersThe target is not a single scalar property but potential-dependent structure and physicochemical behavior at an electrified interface.
Estimating Potential-Dependent Physicochemical Properties at Metal–Electrolyte Interfaces Using Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
Ankit Mathanker et al. · ACS Electrochemistry · Published 13 April 2026
DOI: 10.1021/acselectrochem.5c00540

The electrochemical problem

Metal–electrolyte interfaces reorganize with electrode charge and applied potential. First-principles molecular dynamics can describe this structure with high fidelity, but the accessible length and time scales are too small for many interfacial observables.

Machine-learning interatomic potentials offer a possible bridge: retain near-DFT energy and force accuracy while running molecular dynamics much more cheaply.

What the researchers did

The study develops MACE machine-learning interatomic potentials within an active-learning workflow for aqueous NaCl in contact with Au, Cu, and Rh(111) electrodes. Training data are expanded where the model is uncertain, rather than sampling configuration space blindly.

The final committee of models is tested across 21 metal–electrolyte systems spanning a broad range of surface charge densities.

What they found

The authors report DFT-level accuracy across the 21 systems and use the resulting simulations to estimate potential-dependent physicochemical properties of the interface at scales that would be much more expensive with direct DFT molecular dynamics.

This is important because electrochemical structure is not static: water orientation, ion organization, and interfacial response change as the electrode charge changes.

Why this matters

For atomistic electrochemistry, the bottleneck is often sampling. A theoretically accurate method is of limited use if it cannot reach the configurations and time scales needed for statistical observables.

Active-learning MLIPs provide a route to spend first-principles calculations where they are most informative and then use the learned potential for longer molecular dynamics.

One important caution

Machine-learning potentials inherit a chemical domain from their training data. Good performance across the tested Au, Cu, Rh and NaCl systems does not guarantee reliable extrapolation to different electrode chemistries, adsorbates, reactions, or electrolyte compositions.

Electrochemical potential is also represented through a specific modeling framework. Results should be interpreted within those assumptions rather than as a universal constant-potential simulation method.

Primary source

Ankit Mathanker et al. Estimating Potential-Dependent Physicochemical Properties at Metal–Electrolyte Interfaces Using Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials. ACS Electrochemistry (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acselectrochem.5c00540.
